scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Orunyege-Ntogoro dates to the pre-colonial era of the Bunyoro-Kitara and Tooro kingdoms in western Uganda, where it served as both a social gathering and an athletic courtship contest.
Young people convened during evening social gatherings to dance under moonlight.
Oral traditions recount that when several suitors sought the hand of the same bride, community elders organized an open dance competition.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Entogoro functions as a courtship showcase, community celebration, and instructional medium for transmitting social etiquette.
It is traditionally performed during weddings, youth initiation ceremonies, social gatherings, and Empaako naming rituals.
The dance serves as an educational vehicle, instructing younger generations on community standards regarding courtship, resilience, and mutual respect between partners.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by two ensembles: male dancers (abakwongezi) and female dancers (abakwetegerezi).
Dancers assemble in circles, lines, and paired arrangements, responding to musical cues from the drummers and the omukama (master of ceremonies).
Men execute energetic foot stomps, spins, and jumps that activate their leg rattles, while women perform graceful hip movements that oscillate their beaded waist rings.
Watch for Ebinyege rattle strike, Entogoro hip oscillation, Courting leap.

Formation: Circular staging transitioning into opposing gender lines and advancing couple pairings.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Musical accompaniment is provided by an ensemble of drums, traditional flutes, and xylophones.
The drummers dictate transitions, shifting rhythmic density and tempo in response to the dance's dramatic arc.
Listen for the drums, flutes, xylophones, ebinyege (dried gourd leg rattles).

A dense, driving acoustic texture defined by the sharp, percussive crack of dried gourd leg rattles locked to low- and mid-toned traditional drums. Above the percussive base, wooden xylophone bars and aerophone flutes weave bright counter-melodies, punctuated by dynamic vocal calls, praises, and crowd cheers from the omukama.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Male dancers wear shirts and shorts, with ebinyege—rattles fashioned from dried gourds or calabashes—fastened securely to their legs.
Female dancers wear long skirts and blouses, girded at the waist with entogoro rings made of cowrie shells or beads designed to accentuate hip articulations.
Traditionally performed outdoors on bare earth under moonlight, contemporary performances take place at cultural festivals, wedding receptions, tourism exhibitions, and school auditoriums.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The master of ceremonies, designated as the omukama, serves as the central artistic director of the performance, steering the musicians and dancers through vocal calls.
Ethnomusicologist Linda Cimardi has documented and analyzed the wider runyege performance genre in western Uganda, examining its role in cultural preservation and gender dynamics.

The dance synthesizes two regional forms: Orunyege, hailing from the Hoima and Fort Portal districts, which features highly energetic and acrobatic movements; and Ntogoro, originating from the Masindi district, which emphasizes graceful, fluid, and elegant posturing.
Originating within the ancestral courts and rural settlements of the Bunyoro-Kitara and Tooro kingdoms, the dance is sustained by the Batooro and Banyoro communities.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright yet grounded torso with slightly bent knees to absorb ground impacts and facilitate rapid leg shaking.
Open, expressive gestures framing the torso, balanced outward for stability during jumping and spinning.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Stomp the right foot into the floor to sound the leg rattle (ebinyege) on the downbeat.
Step 2: Transfer weight smoothly to the left foot while engaging a quick rebound strike.
Footwork from the sources: Percussive downward stomps, rapid heel-toe shakes, weight shifts, and grounded pivots designed to sound leg rattles.
Drill: Practice stationary right-foot downbeat stomps with bent knees.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Isolate and circle the hips rhythmically so the waist ring (entogoro) swings laterally.
Step 4: Execute an explosive vertical hop, landing simultaneously on both feet to produce a unified rattle crash.
Drill: Alternate four stomps on the right with four on the left.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Add soft hand claps to internalize the drum accent.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Avoid stiffening the knees or landing flat-footed when wearing rattles to protect the joints during high jumps.
